text:
acme-dev: Hey team — since yesterday around 14:30 UTC our production service started getting intermittent 429s from the Redwood Dedicated endpoint. We have a reserved pool (pool-id: rp_42) on eu-west and our SLA expects steady throughput for chat requests. Any idea?

Ava (Support): Thanks for flagging. Can you paste a short sample of the failing request headers and the exact 429 body if available? Also which model and config (max_tokens, streaming on/off)?

acme-dev: Sample header and response below. Model: redwood-medium-1, streaming=false
```
POST /v1/generate
Authorization: Bearer sk-REDACTED
X-Redwood-Pool: rp_42
Content-Type: application/json
User-Agent: acme-service/2.1.0
```
Response: 429 Too Many Requests {"error":"rate_exceeded","retry_after":null}

Riley (CS): Noted. Was this correlated with a deployment or a traffic spike? Any traffic shaping on your side?

acme-dev: We had a small canary deploy but traffic was steady — about 200 requests/sec (avg) with occasional bursts to ~600 rps for ~10s. No client-side throttles other than exponential backoff.

Diego (Oncall Runtime): I can pull request logs from the dedicated pool. Initial thought: reserved pool has a throughput cap per-second and a short burst window; if bursts exceed the burst budget we return 429s. I'll check rp_42 config.

CapacityBot: Pool rp_42 config snapshot: capacity_qps: 500, burst_window_s: 30, burst_allowance_tokens: 8000, sla_target_p99_latency_ms: 250

Maya (SRE): If capacity_qps is 500 and sustained was 200 but bursts to 600 for 10s, that could exceed both sustained and burst allowance depending on token accounting. What are your average tokens per request?

acme-dev: ~120 tokens per request on average. So at 600 rps that's ~72k tokens/s, but I guess Redwood's qps is request-based not token-based? We assumed token-based earlier.

Ava (Support): To clarify: Dedicated pool rate caps are enforced both at the request level and at a token-throughput heuristic in the runtime. The primary limiter is requests/sec for concurrency shaping, but long requests with large token output can consume kv-cache and kernel slots and therefore contribute to a virtual token budget.

Diego (Oncall Runtime): I pulled the runtime logs for rp_42 around the timestamps. Quick excerpt:
```
[2026-03-15T14:30:12Z] pool=rp_42 req_id=abc123 client=acme-service rps_window=10 avg_rps=320 cap_qps=500 burst_allowance_remain=4000 -> allowed
[2026-03-15T14:32:05Z] pool=rp_42 req_id=def456 client=acme-service rps_window=10 avg_rps=580 cap_qps=500 burst_allowance_remain=200 -> rate_exceeded -> 429
[2026-03-15T14:32:15Z] pool=rp_42 req_id=ghi789 client=acme-service rps_window=10 avg_rps=610 cap_qps=500 burst_allowance_remain=-150 -> rate_exceeded -> 429
```
Diego (Oncall Runtime): Looks like bursts consumed the burst_allowance quickly; the allocator then started returning 429s. The negative allowance indicates the implementation allows temporary negative allowance to mark overshoot and then rejects until refill.

acme-dev: Hmm — our understanding was that Dedicated supports short bursts well above the cap for short durations. Is there a discrepancy between what's documented and the runtime?

Riley (CS): We had a doc note that burst windows are for small, short spikes but not arbitrarily high bursts. I'll pull the public doc link. In the meantime, Diego — any tracing that shows which requests were large (tokens) or long (latency) that might have contributed more to allowance consumption?

Diego (Oncall Runtime): Yes — trace shows a subset of requests with max_tokens=1024 (we're seeing both short and long requests). Long responses hold the kernel and KV cache longer and count more heavily in the scheduler. Those coincide with the highest burst moments.

Maya (SRE): Two root causes likely: (1) a mismatch between client burst shape and the configured burst policy (burst_window/allowance) for rp_42, and (2) presence of long/high-token requests that eat more runtime resources. Action items: adjust pool config OR throttle long-response requests client-side OR add an additional reserved pool to handle bursts.

acme-dev: We prefer not to change the client. Can you explain what changing pool config means? Does it impact cost or SLA?

Ava (Support): Options: (A) Increase capacity_qps for rp_42 (reduces 429s but costs more reserved capacity). (B) Increase burst_allowance_tokens and/or burst_window_s to tolerate larger but short spikes (moderate cost; still bounded). (C) Add a secondary reserved pool and set routing policy to prefer rp_42 then fallback to rp_43 for bursts (recommended for high-variance traffic). Any config change can affect billing because reserved capacity is a committed cost; burst allowance sizing is part of pool tier.

Diego (Oncall Runtime): Quick reproduction steps we used to confirm behavior (shareable):
1) Send steady 200 rps with small requests (50 tokens) -> no 429s.
2) Inject spike to 600 rps for 12s with 120-token requests -> 429s begin at ~8s into spike.
3) Repeat with same spike but split long requests (1k tokens) -> allowance drains faster and 429s appear earlier.
```
# simple repro script (pseudocode)
for t in range(0,120):
  rps = 200 if t<30 or t>60 else 600
  send_requests(rps, tokens=120)
```
Maya (SRE): Temporary mitigation we can apply quickly: increase burst_allowance_tokens by 50% for rp_42 and bump capacity_qps to 700 for 24 hours while we monitor. acme-dev — want us to proceed with a short trial week?

acme-dev: Yes please. We need minimal disruption. Also we'd like better visibility into pool metrics (burst allowance, current allowance, per-client bucket) in Console. Right now we only see aggregate QPS and latency.

Riley (CS): Logged feature request for more granular pool metrics to Product/Console team. Ticket REF-987.

Ava (Support): I'll schedule the trial change for rp_42: capacity_qps -> 700, burst_allowance_tokens -> 12000 for 24h starting 2026-03-16T06:00Z. We'll monitor and report back p99 latency and 429 rate.

CapacityBot: Scheduled pool update rp_42 @ 2026-03-16T06:00Z by Ava. Change-id: chg_8812. Monitoring: enabled.

Diego (Oncall Runtime): Post-change checks: if 429s drop to near-zero during similar spikes, we confirm config was the main limiter. If not, we'll dig deeper into kernel-level contention and KV cache eviction.

acme-dev: Thanks team. One last ask — can you document recommended client-side throttles/headers we should set to play nicer with dedicated pools? For example do you prefer a Retry-After header or should we use exponential backoff with jitter?

Ava (Support): Best practice: implement client-side leaky-bucket shaping to keep sustained QPS under capacity_qps, allow short bursts that match your pool's burst_window, and on 429s respect Retry-After if present otherwise use exponential backoff with full-jitter. We'll send a quick guidance snippet after the trial starts.

Maya (SRE): Follow-up: created internal postmortem checklist entry to verify pool config docs reflect token-vs-request accounting and to add console metrics. (internal-ref: PMT-452)

Ava (Support): I'll update thread after the 24h trial completes. For now: scheduled change, repro confirmed, root cause = burst allowance exhaustion (combined effect of request bursts + high-token responses).

acme-dev: Great — appreciate the fast turnaround :thumbsup:

(reacts: Ava (Support) :thumbsup:, Riley (CS) :eyes:, Diego (Oncall Runtime) :wrench: )
